units: a rehabilitation specialist describes two opposite attitudes among the people she treats
the first attitude consists in locking the injured joint and never using it again
the second attitude consists in wanting to pull on the muscle from the very first appointment
the specialist judges that neither of these ways of behaving is right
the absence of movement ends up weakening the joint and hardening the muscle attachments
an effort that is too violent prolongs the irritation of the tissues
a colleague points out that the same uncertainty shows up with injuries to the hand
the two practitioners recommend moderate and frequent movements, stopped in case of strong pain
they recall that recovery is judged over several weeks and not over a single appointment
text: A physiotherapist says her patients turn up believing one of two contrary things about healing. Some want a sore ankle strapped into a rigid splint and left well alone until it settles of its own accord. Others ask to be stretched at the very first session, convinced that soreness is proof they are getting better. Neither approach works, she says. Keep a joint still for too long and it grows weak while the tendons stiffen; push too hard and the swelling simply carries on. A colleague of hers adds that the same muddle crops up among people who have hurt a wrist. What helps, the two of them argue, is small movements done often, and stopped the moment the pain turns sharp. They end on the point their patients tend to skip: recovery is measured over whole weeks, never over a single appointment.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the healers of former times relied on an oral inheritance for want of reliable devices
this know-how was limited to a small number of practices
plant drinks were used against fever and against irritation of the throat
fragrant ointments were applied to the swollen areas
warm poultices were laid on at bedtime and taken off on rising
the drawing of blood was both dreaded and demanded
the healer's speech weighed as much as his preparations
the act of giving the illness a name already brought relief
science has kept few of these treatments but has drawn from them a lesson about waiting and trust
text: Long before healers had instruments they could trust, they leaned on what had been handed down by word of mouth alone, and that inheritance amounted to no more than a small handful of remedies. First came the brewed drinks: a bitter one to bring down a fever, a sweetened one to soothe a throat rubbed raw. Then the ointments, spread thickly over swollen skin, whose sharp smell was half the cure. Warm poultices followed, laid on at bedtime and lifted away at first light. Bleeding stood apart from the rest, dreaded and demanded by turns. And the healer's own voice counted for as much as anything he mixed: he gave the illness a name, and the naming of it already brought ease. From that tangled legacy medicine has kept very few treatments, though it did draw from it a lasting lesson about waiting and about trust.

units: the medicine in the form of a shell first goes down the passage leading to the stomach
contractions of the muscles carry out this descent
the acidity of the stomach dissolves the shell and releases its contents
the folded wall of the fine bowel takes up the active matter
the blood then carries the matter towards the organ that transforms it
this transformation lowers the strength of the remedy
the remaining part attaches to precise targets in the tissues concerned
the action rises to a peak then decreases as elimination goes on
a liquid preparation acts sooner because its active matter is already in solution
text: A swallowed capsule passes through several stages before it can do anything at all. It travels down the gullet, driven along by steady waves of muscle. In the stomach the acid juices break the shell open and release the powder held inside. From there the contents reach the small bowel, whose deeply folded lining offers an enormous surface for taking things up. The drug crosses into the blood, which carries it onwards to the liver; that organ alters part of the molecule and weakens its effect. Whatever survives travels on to the tissues it was meant for, and locks onto particular receptors there. The effect builds, peaks, then fades as the kidneys and the liver clear the substance away. A syrup takes much the same route, but starts working sooner, since the drug held in it is already dissolved.

units: a player of a stringed instrument sought advice for headaches that cut his playing sessions short
no disorder was found on the side of the eyes or the ears
the practitioner spotted a clenching of the jaws during difficult passages
this repeated clenching exhausted the muscles lying between the skull and the neck
the tension spread towards the sides of the forehead and brought on the pain
the fear of the attacks increased the contraction and kept the trouble going
the practitioner taught the musician a short release between two pieces played
she added to it an exercise of deep breathing
the headaches became rarer after one season
the musician put his trouble down to the fear of failure rather than to his instrument
text: A violinist went to see a practitioner because headaches were cutting his practice short. Nothing was wrong with his eyes, and nothing was wrong with his hearing. What she did notice was that he clenched his jaw the moment a difficult passage came up. Repeated over whole sessions at a stretch, that clenching wore out the muscles running from the skull down into the neck, and the strain then spread up to the temples, where the pain began. Because he dreaded the attacks, he tightened all the more, and so the trouble kept feeding itself. She taught him a brief release to use between one piece and the next, along with an exercise in slow and deep breathing. Within a single season the headaches had grown rare. The musician concluded that his instrument mattered less than his own fear of failing on it.

units: an unpleasant mouth smell on waking rarely comes from the stomach
it is caused above all by micro-organisms that multiply on the tongue and near the gums during sleep
the method proposed involves five actions that can be carried out without costly equipment
the teeth must be cleaned on waking and before sleeping, turning the brush towards the flesh of the gums
a thread must pass between the teeth because the brush does not reach those gaps
the tongue must be scraped gently to remove the pale film that forms on it
drinking water helps because a dry mouth sharpens the smell whereas saliva cleans
an appointment with the dental practitioner is needed if the trouble carries on
inflamed gums or a damaged tooth can keep the trouble going without being visible
text: Bad breath on waking worries a good many people, though it rarely starts in the stomach. It comes mostly from the bacteria multiplying overnight on the tongue and along the gum line. The remedy amounts to five simple habits, none of which calls for costly equipment. Brush on rising and again at bedtime, angling the bristles towards the gum rather than scrubbing away at the enamel alone. Then run floss between the teeth, since a brush can never reach those narrow gaps. Scrape the surface of the tongue gently, where a pale film gathers. Drink water steadily through the day: a dry mouth sharpens the smell, whereas saliva rinses it away. If the problem carries on despite all this, see a dentist, because inflamed gums or a damaged tooth can keep it going without ever showing themselves.

units: two opposite opinions circulate in a neighbourhood gym
one group defends sessions in a very hot cabin
these enthusiasts claim that their muscles loosen after sweating heavily
the other group prefers immersion in very cold water
the latter maintain that the pain disappears abruptly
the instructor of the place refuses to side with either of the two camps
he explains that heat softens and stirs up the circulation of the blood
he explains that cold numbs and soothes the irritation of the tissues
according to him the two methods suit different moments
he judges that sleeping enough and drinking enough counts for more than these practices
text: In a gym round the corner you can hear two camps going at each other flat out. On one side, the heat people: one session after another in a scorching cabin, and out they come dripping wet, swearing blind that every last muscle has come undone. On the other, the cold lot, who drop themselves into a tub of icy water and reckon the ache switches off all at once. The coach, for his part, just grins and sends the pair of them packing. Heat loosens you up and gets the blood moving, he points out, while cold numbs the part and settles down the swelling; both have their moment, only never the same one. What he mostly notices is that the regulars forget the plain basics: enough sleep and enough water. No cabin on earth, he laughs, makes up for short nights and meals bolted down standing.

units: the care premises are on the floor above a food shop
they comprise two rooms with little furniture
the reception room holds only seats, a plant and worn magazines
the second room is used for consultations and houses a table covered with paper, a weighing device and an instrument for measuring pressure
the boxes of medicines are stored up high and sorted by illness
the clean equipment is kept in a drawer, each injection instrument in sealed wrapping
the tap of the basin is opened with the arm to limit the passing on of germs
the nurse receives people without an appointment on three half-days a week
she treats wounds, changes dressings and listens to the fears of those who come
the place is very quiet, only the cold storage device makes a noise
text: The surgery takes up two rooms above a grocer's shop, and nothing in it is surplus to need. The waiting area holds a row of chairs, a green plant and a pile of dog-eared magazines, and that is the whole of it. Next door is where people are examined: a narrow couch covered over in paper, an old set of scales, a blood pressure gauge fixed to the wall. Boxes of tablets sit on the topmost shelf, sorted out by complaint. A drawer holds the sterile kit, every syringe still sealed up in its sachet. By the window stands a basin whose tap is worked with the elbow, which keeps germs from travelling about. The nurse who runs the place takes people without appointments on three afternoons a week; she dresses wounds, changes bandages and listens to people's worries. The quiet in there is thick, broken only by the hum of the fridge.

units: night rest was first despised before being reconsidered
it was held at the start to be an empty gap that had to be shortened
active minds believed themselves obliged to sleep less
a later phase valued long waking hours as a mark of courage
exhaustion was then displayed as a distinction
studies carried out at night then showed intense activity in the sleeping brain
this activity includes sorting, the fixing of memories and repair
of late we count our nights and worry about a result judged poor
the writer holds that this counted watching is a mistake
he maintains that rest calls for steadiness, for darkness and for a calm mind
text: Sleep fell out of favour for a long stretch of time before it was taken seriously again, and the journey is worth pausing over for a moment. It was held at first to be an empty gap, a mere parenthesis stolen from a life, which anyone of industrious mind had a plain duty to cut short. Then came the age of the guilty sleeper: staying up late proved your mettle, and exhaustion was worn about like a badge. Later the laboratories were opened at night, and there we found a brain hard at work, sorting, fixing memories in place, mending. Lately the pendulum has swung back the other way: we count our nights, we score them, and we fret over a poor result. That strikes me as a mistake. Rest asks for no heroics and for no supervision; it asks for regular hours, for darkness and for a mind at ease.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the head of a healing plant workshop had not intended this line of work
a lasting allergic reaction, poorly soothed, pushed her to take an interest in the make-up of plant drinks
this interest led her to study plants and then to work in a place of analysis
she observed that the richness of plants changes with the nature of the ground and the moment of picking
she therefore made a check of every batch compulsory before it dries
this rule lowered her rate of production
impatient buyers left her because of these delays
the sellers of medicines trust her and take the greater part of her output
she refuses to announce cures and recalls that a plant drink soothes without treating an infection
her colleagues put the long life of the business down to this restraint
text: The woman who runs the medicinal herb workshop never set out to do this kind of work. A stubborn allergy that ordinary treatments barely touched led her to look closely at what actually went into the herbal drinks she kept being offered. That curiosity took her into the study of plants, and from there into an analysis laboratory. Since she could see that plant strength varies with the soil and with the timing of the harvest, she made a test of every single batch compulsory before drying. The rule slowed her output and drove away buyers in a hurry; in exchange it won her the trust of chemists, who now take the greater part of what she produces. She still refuses to promise cures: a herbal drink soothes, it does not clear an infection. That restraint, her staff say, is why the workshop has lasted so long.

units: a prevention scheme aimed at the staff of a company receives a mixed appraisal
the opening analysis is judged accurate
sitting still in front of a screen hardens the neck and dulls the shoulders
it also brings on pains at the joint of the hand that remedies do not wipe out for long
the solution chosen is a sound signal that cuts off the activity and suggests a short loosening exercise
the first reactions report reduced discomfort at the end of the week
the carrying out is criticised for its lack of flexibility
the signal goes off without taking account of the attention under way
many employees switch the device off after a week
the writer proposes letting each person set their own break times and adopting a discreet visual reminder
text: The prevention scheme offered to the staff at this company deserves a mixed verdict. Its opening analysis is sound enough: fixed postures in front of a screen stiffen the neck, dull the shoulders and bring on a wrist pain that no medicine clears away for long. The answer devised is an audible alert that halts the task in hand and proposes a short stretch. The idea appeals, and the early reports mention less discomfort by the end of the week. The way it has been carried out, though, is rigid: the alert goes off with no regard at all for whatever the person is concentrating on, and a good many employees switch it off altogether after a week. A remedy looks within reach, namely to let each person set their own break times, and to replace the sound with a discreet reminder on the screen.
